claims.text: The target alloy is a high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements, each at 5–35 at%.
Titanium and nickel are primary constituents of the target alloy.
Standard melting or additive manufacturing can produce this alloy as a largely homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
A solution treatment followed by aging at 700–900 °C for 2–4 hours can induce nanoscale coherent intermetallic precipitates in the titanium- and nickel-primary alloy.
The induced intermetallic precipitates will be analogous to the gamma-prime phase.
The heat treatment will produce uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates coherently embedded in the primary solid-solution matrix.
The coherent precipitates will obstruct or pin dislocations.
Obstructing dislocation motion will suppress high-temperature plastic deformation.
The precipitates will suppress creep at elevated temperature.
The heat-treated alloy will have a statistically significant increase in elevated-temperature yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will have a lower elevated-temperature creep rate than the untreated alloy.
The strengthening effect applies below a precipitate dissolution limit likely around 1000–1200 °C.
At temperatures outside the proposed operating boundary, the precipitates may coarsen or dissolve.
Precipitate coarsening or dissolution will reduce the strengthening effect.
The optimal aging temperature, aging time, precipitate volume fraction, and precipitate coherence are not yet known.
The long-term thermal stability of the induced precipitates under service conditions is uncertain.
